My name is Jeff Cloud. I served as an elected member of the Oklahoma Corporation
Commission (“Commission”) for eight years from January 2003 until October 2011. During my
tenure at the Commission, I served as Chairman from 2005-2009. I also represented the state of
Oklahoma on the Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) Regional State Committee from 2007-
2011. During my tenure on the Commission, SPP became a FERC-approved Regional
Transmission Organization; implemented its first regional energy imbalance market, and began
the groundwork of implementing its current 14 state competitive wholesale market, the SPP
Integrated Marketplace. I have served on the Electricity Committee for the National Association
of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (“NARUC”), the Joint Boards on Security Constrained
Economic Dispatch, and the Advisory Board for the Center for Public Utilities at New Mexico
State University. I am intimately familiar with the issues and problems that Oklahoma faces with
regard to ensuring that rates are affordable and reliability is maintained.

I currently serve as the Executive Director of the Alliance for Secure Energy, a non-profit
organization created to ensure that Oklahomans have secure, affordable and reliable electric energy
now and in the future. The Alliance for Secure Energy supports policies and regulations that
impact infrastructure expansion and upgrades, new electric generation, environmental
stewardship, economic development, sustainability, and affordability. It is critical to
advance policies in Oklahoma that balance the important goals of keeping energy prices
affordable and ensuring utilities remain financially secure so they can continue to invest in
infrastructure and provide reliable service.

I recently reviewed the September 4, 2026 public comments filed in Case Nos. PUD 2026-
000046, and PUD2025-000075 by Nick Coffey, a Democrat political candidate. I felt compelled
to file reply comments because of the inaccuracies and misstatements contained in Mr. Coffey’s
filing and the lack of understanding of the law and facts.

The comment filed by Mr. Coffey rests on two mistaken premises: (1) that the White House
Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary policy statement, defines the legal standard applicable to
this proceeding rather than Oklahoma House Bill 2992 (“HB 2992”), and (2) that OG&E’s XLPL
tariff limits large-load customers to paying only the “direct” cost of grid interconnection. Neither
premise survives review of the record OG&E has established in Case No. PUD2026-000046,
including the Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop, Gwin Cash, and Matthew DeCourcey. Nor
does the comment account for the substantial downward pressure that XLPL customers will place
on rates for every existing customer by paying their share of the system’s fixed costs.

As discussed below, there are several problems with Mr. Coffey’s unsupported assertions:

e Mr. Coffey conflates two different documents with two different legal statuses. HB 2992
is Oklahoma statutory law; the White House Pledge is a voluntary commitment with no
independent force under Oklahoma law and no role in defining the Commission’s
ratemaking standard in this docket.

e An independent, cross-utility comparison shows OG&E’s customer protections are the
strongest, or among the strongest, on every major metric.


 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 30 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/09/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 6

e An independent consultant concluded that OG&E’s proposal provides customer
protections that are more robust than in other parts of the United States.

e The tariff goes beyond “hold harmless” and affirmatively creates benefits for residential

customers.

e Under OG&E’s proposal, every dollar of shared, fixed system cost that an XLPL customer
pays is a dollar that OG&E's residential, commercial, and industrial customers do not have
to pay. That is not a marginal or speculative benefit — it is a direct, near-mechanical
consequence of how utility rates are set, and it is documented at length in the record.

II. The Comment Misstates What HB 2992 Requires

The central argument advanced by Mr. Coffey is that HB 2992 — which the comment calls
“Oklahoma’s Ratepayer Act” — only protects customers “from paying unjust rates resulting
directly from electric service to large load customers,” and that this means data centers are “only
required to pay for added costs resulting directly from their new operations,” i.e., interconnection
costs alone. That is not what HB 2992 requires, and it is not how OG&E has implemented it.

As OG&E witness Kimber Shoop explains, HB 2992 (codified at 17 Okla. Stat. §§ 901—
905, effective July 1, 2026) requires electric utilities to “establish and maintain separate terms,
conditions, and tariffs applicable to large load customers, including credit requirements and other
measures necessary to ensure that such customers reimburse the electric supplier for all costs fairly
allocated to them, and that the term of service for a large load customer be at least ten years.” That
is a cost-causation and cost-allocation standard — not a narrow “direct connection cost” limitation.
Nothing in the statutory text cited by Mr. Coffey confines recoverable costs to interconnection; it
directs utilities to ensure large-load customers bear the costs “fairly allocated” to them, however
those costs arise.

OG&E witness Gwin Cash confirms this is exactly how the Company built the tariff. Mr.
Cash testifies that the tariffs Customer Class Protection Charge — reviewed and, if necessary,
reset in every general rate case — functions as “a tariff-embedded fail-safe mechanism that ensures
the cost causation principles required by Oklahoma House Bill 2992 are reviewed often, and
enforced on an ongoing basis.” That is a standing, recurring compliance mechanism tied directly
to the statute, which will continuously protect customers from any possible adverse effects, should
they occur.

The comment filed by Mr. Coffey conflates two different documents with two different
legal statuses. HB 2992 is Oklahoma statutory law; the White House Pledge is a voluntary
commitment with no independent force under Oklahoma law and no role in defining the
Commission’s ratemaking standard in this docket. The Commission’s task in PUD2026-000046
is to determine whether OG&E’s tariff satisfies HB 2992 and sound cost-of-service principles —
not whether it tracks language from a White House press release. On that statutory question, the
record shows OG&E’s tariff goes beyond the “fairly allocated” standard requires, as explained
below.

 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 30 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/09/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 6

reduce the average cost to serve each customer,” because “existing system costs will be spread
over many more kilowatt-hours, resulting in all retail customers on the system paying less per
kilowatt-hour.” As he summarizes, “the new loads ... put downward pressure on rates for all
customer classes, including residential, commercial, and industrial customers.”

Mr. DeCourcey’s testimony explains the mechanism in more detail. Because OG&E’s rate
structure requires large-load customers to fund the costs incurred specifically to serve them
(through CIAC payments and minimum billing obligations) while also contributing to the utility’s
shared, fixed system costs, XLPL customers both pay their own way and help defray costs that
would otherwise fall entirely on existing classes. As Mr. DeCourcey puts it, “all else equal, growth
in utility sales tends to decrease rates,” and the result of adding XLPL load under this tariff
structure “is lower rates for OG&E’s existing customers.” As a former Commissioner, it is quite
clear to me that this is why the regulated utility system we have in Oklahoma works so well. We
have regulatory oversight to ensure that costs are allocated fairly with the proper accountability to
ensure reliability is maximized and a growing customer base helps keep rates affordable.

This is not a theoretical prediction unique to OG&E. Mr. DeCourcey’s testimony catalogs
the same finding by regulators and utilities across the country that have recently authorized large-
load tariffs, each concluding that spreading fixed costs over greater sales volume benefits existing
customers:

The Michigan Public Service Commission approved a large-load tariff for Consumers
Energy in part because “additional demand represented by data centers and other customers
could potentially benefit all customers by spreading out the fixed costs of the utility’s
electric grid over a larger amount of grid usage.”

Tucson Electric Power explained to its regulator that because usage-based rates are
calculated by dividing fixed costs by projected energy sales, adding a large customer
“results in lower usage-based rates” for everyone else.

Georgia Power has committed to demonstrating savings of at least $8.50 per month for
residential customers as a result of serving new large loads.

Evergy stated that its newly approved large-load tariffs ensure new customers “pay their
fair share of existing and new system costs,” which “will drive affordability benefits for
existing customers.”

Pacific Gas and Electric calculated that for every 1,000 MW of new large-load demand
added under its tariff, total costs for existing customers decline by 1—2 percent, because
“spreading the costs over more units of energy” means “each customer’s dollar can go
further.”

OG&E’s own record evidence, cited by Mr. DeCourcey, reaches the identical conclusion:
in Case No. PUD2026-000031, OG&E witness Jason Thenmadathil updated the Company’s
Commission-approved cost-of-service study to include a large-load customer while holding all
other factors constant, and confirmed that the addition “put downward pressure on rates for
existing customers.”

 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 30 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/09/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 6

And this benefit is layered on top of — not instead of — the customer-specific protections
described in Section II above. The XLPL tariff does not ask existing customers to choose between
protection from cost-shifting and a share of the benefit of new load; the tariffs CIAC, minimum
billing, and stranded-cost provisions ensure XLPL customers pay their own way in full, and their
contribution to shared system costs reduces what every other customer pays. Mr. Coffey’s
comment addresses neither half of this benefit, and in doing so presents an incomplete — and
materially misleading — picture of how the XLPL tariff will actually affect Oklahoma ratepayers.

V. Conclusion

The comment filed by Mr. Coffey reads HB 2992 as capping large-load cost responsibility
at interconnection costs and treats the White House Pledge as the applicable legal standard.
Neither reading is supported by the statute or by the record in this case. HB 2992 requires that
large-load customers reimburse utilities for costs “fairly allocated” to them — a standard OG&E’s
XLPL tariff meets and exceeds through 100% T&D cost recovery (including future upgrades), a
15-year minimum term with binding exit fees, industry-leading minimum billing floors, substantial
collateral requirements, a recurring Customer Class Protection Charge, and an affirmative, multi-
hundred-million-dollar Customer Affordability Charge benefiting residential customers
specifically.

On top of these customer-specific protections, XLPL customers will also help pay down
the fixed costs shared by every class on OG&E’s system, putting downward pressure on rates for
all existing customers — a significant, well-documented benefit that the comment overlooks
entirely. I respectfully requests that the Commission evaluate the XLPL tariff against the standard
Oklahoma law sets, and approve it as filed for being good for customers.

Respectfully submitted,
